documents.title: AI Teaching and Research Guidance
documents.summary: Short CFE page stating OU's approach to AI in teaching and research, pointing faculty to a Canvas course, consultations and AI literacy frameworks. It sets no rule on student AI use.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'OU does not mandate a single approach to AI in the classroom' and that faculty make discipline-appropriate choices and communicate them, so the decision is handed to instructors and the document sets no stance of its own.

units.why: States 'OU does not mandate a single approach', so no university rule on AI use is set and the choice is left to faculty; this is a decision-delegation (P04), directed to instructors in course design.
units.anchor: OU does not mandate a single approach to AI in the classroom.

units.why: Faculty are 'encouraged to make intentional, discipline-appropriate choices', placing the decision with instructors and discipline; phrased as encouragement so modality is should.
units.anchor: faculty are encouraged to make intentional, discipline-appropriate choices

units.why: Faculty are told 'to communicate those choices clearly to students', which is about making expectations explicit at the start; closest is P09 though it does not say in the syllabus specifically.
units.anchor: to communicate those choices clearly to students
units.policy: Faculty are encouraged to communicate their AI choices clearly to students.
units.fit_note: Does not say the statement must be in the syllabus; only that choices be communicated clearly.

units.why: Frames AI as raising 'important questions about learning goals, assessment, authorship, and academic integrity'; a general statement of the issues, not a rule. A framework preamble (P56) is the nearest type but fits only partly.
units.anchor: AI raises important questions about learning goals, assessment, authorship, and academic integrity.
units.fit_note: Names the concerns AI raises but sets no purpose, scope or principles.

units.why: The CFE offers a Canvas course on generative AI and teaching; this is faculty-facing learning support (P63), not a rule.
units.anchor: The CFE has developed a Canvas course called Generative AI at the University

units.why: The Canvas course supplies 'example Generative AI Policy language for your syllabus', i.e. templates instructors can adopt (P110).
units.anchor: example Generative AI Policy language for your syllabus

units.why: Offers consultations on AI to faculty, a support service matching P63 (workshops, consultations).
units.anchor: Faculty members can also schedule consultations on AI

units.why: Points faculty to 'workshops and learning communities' on AI, which is P63 faculty support.
units.anchor: CFE workshops and learning communities on AI-related topics

units.why: Faculty are 'encouraged to consider how AI affects assignment design, assessment strategies' and learning; this asks for redesign thinking (P35) rather than prescribing a change, hence a fit note.
units.anchor: consider how AI affects assignment design, assessment strategies
units.fit_note: Asks faculty to consider the effect on assignment design; does not prescribe a redesign.

units.why: The listed AI literacy frameworks (Digital Education Council, UNESCO, etc.) are offered as resources for course outcomes and design; this points readers to further guidance (P115) rather than saying anything about AI use.
units.anchor: These frameworks can inform course outcomes, assignment design

units.why: Faculty are 'encouraged to consult OU guidance and campus experts before integrating AI into research workflows or grant proposals'; this is AI in research and grants (P62), as a soft should.
units.anchor: encouraged to consult OU guidance and campus experts before integrating AI

units.why: A named CFE faculty fellow for AI offers appointments; this is faculty support (P63) for research and AI questions.
units.anchor: the CFE has a faculty fellow specifically for AI-related subjects.

units.why: Says consultations 'do not require a commitment to using AI', lowering the barrier to seek help; part of faculty support (P63).
units.anchor: do not require a commitment to using AI in a project

documents.title: Generative AI Policy examples (July 2025)
documents.summary: CFE sample syllabus statements for instructors at six levels based on the AI Assessment Scale, from restricted use to full use and exploration, plus a per-assignment version. Each includes a rationale, implementation, consequences and a statement of the instructor's own AI use.
documents.stance_why: The document offers six sample policies ('five policy examples based on the AI Assessment Scale ... and a sixth' per-assignment) for instructors to adopt or mix, so it sets no single stance and delegates, listing the tiers.

units.why: Instructors are 'encouraged to have Generative AI policies for each assignment', which sets rules per assignment (P04) and asks for explicit statements.
units.anchor: you are encouraged to have Generative AI policies for each assignment in your class.

units.why: The heading calls a Generative AI policy a 'required component' of the syllabus, which may sit in academic-integrity language if explicit; this is a syllabus-statement requirement (P09).
units.anchor: required component, text may vary and could be included, as long as it is explicit

units.why: Gives the reason for assignment-level policies: it 'will help reduce confusion among students'; this explains why to discuss and explain rules (P66).
units.anchor: help reduce confusion among students about what is appropriate versus inappropriate usage.

units.why: Even under a ban, instructors are told to explain 'how Generative AI could, but shouldn't, be used, and why'; this is explaining rules to students (P66).
units.anchor: explaining how Generative AI could, but shouldn’t, be used, and why, on specific assignments

units.why: Notes AI is 'increasingly integrated into search tools, e-books, Microsoft and Google products'; a fact about embedded AI that bears on bans, so P07 is the nearest type, as information only.
units.anchor: Generative AI is increasingly integrated into search tools, e-books, Microsoft and Google products
units.fit_note: States the fact of embedded AI as the reason to explain rules; does not itself cover or require disabling it.

units.why: Provides 'five policy examples based on the AI Assessment Scale' plus a per-assignment one: named levels of AI use (P05); the document offers tiers so stance is delegates.
units.anchor: five policy examples based on the AI Assessment Scale

units.why: Instructors may 'mix and match' sample statements to fit course goals; this ties the AI rule to course goals (P83) and adoption of templates.
units.anchor: mix and match the sample statements to more closely align with your course goals
units.fit_note: Aligns the policy to course goals and pedagogy but no learning-objective rule is stated.

units.why: The scale may be applied to single assessments or across the course; this lets the rule be set per assessment or per course (P04).
units.anchor: may also be used across your course, if appropriate.

units.why: Tells instructors to 'modify the list of Generative AI models' to fit their discipline; sample-language adaptation (P110).
units.anchor: please modify the list of Generative AI models to suit your discipline

units.why: Gives the reason for the ban: 'we learn best when we are actively engaged in the process'; AI shortcuts the practice that builds skill (P41).
units.anchor: We learn best when we are actively engaged in the process of completing all aspects

units.why: Argues brainstorming and drafting are an 'integral part of your learning', so they should not be outsourced; fits P41.
units.anchor: Even the brainstorming and initial draft phase is a time of discovery

units.why: Use of named tools 'is considered a violation of the academic integrity policy'; this is the default ban on AI for the course (P01), with misconduct classification secondary.
units.anchor: is considered a violation of the academic integrity policy for this course.

units.why: Spells out prohibited uses: 'write outlines, conduct research, to write or edit your papers', so even editing and research are banned; the unit is about having AI help produce work (P19), and the quiz and exam part is a separate unit under P22.
units.anchor: this includes using Generative AI to write outlines, conduct research, to write or edit your

units.why: The ban names taking 'quizzes or exams' with AI; exam use is P22.
units.anchor: and to take your quizzes or exams.

units.why: Covers search engines and e-books with integrated AI: do 'not rely on the Generative AI output'; embedded AI (P07), with a should-not.
units.anchor: you should not rely on the Generative AI output and engage instead with the source

units.why: Assignments are designed 'to occur in a controlled environment (such as in-class or with Lockdown Browser)' or to resist AI; this shifts weight toward controlled assessment (P33) and redesign.
units.anchor: assignments have been designed to either occur in a controlled environment

units.why: Directs students to the Academic Success Center, Writing Center and other support instead of AI; human help alongside AI (P72).
units.anchor: Academic Success Center, the Writing Center, Bibliographic, Citation, and Reference Management Software

units.why: Even in the ban, 'simple grammar or spell check tools' are listed as acceptable resources; routine features exempted (P100).
units.anchor: and simple grammar or spell check tools.

units.why: Invites students to contact the instructor with questions; P10 (ask before using) is nearest but here it is a general invitation.
units.anchor: reach out to me if you have any questions or concerns.
units.fit_note: General invitation to ask questions, not specifically before using AI.

units.why: Students unsure about 'what counts as Generative AI' should 'talk with me' (the instructor): ask when unsure (P10).
units.anchor: what counts as Generative AI, please talk with me.

units.why: States specific penalties: 'a zero for an assignment or a failing grade on the course'; concrete penalties in advance (P37), though the misconduct class is also stated.
units.anchor: could result in a zero for an assignment or a failing grade on the course.

units.why: The instructor commits to not using AI 'in my teaching, grading, or in my communication'; a commitment stated to students that limits instructor use (P47).
units.anchor: I will not use Generative AI to aid in my teaching, grading, or in my
units.fit_note: A no-use commitment rather than disclosure of actual use; also covers grading (P46).

units.why: Advises placing the policy in the integrity statement or a stand-alone policy; about where to state AI rules in the syllabus (P09).
units.anchor: we encourage you to either integrate this policy into your academic integrity statement or to

units.why: Says AI 'can be very useful' for planning an assignment, which is a statement of benefit (P87).
units.anchor: Generative AI can be very useful as you plan your strategy for how to approach

units.why: Names a specific tool for breaking tasks into steps for planning; AI for planning and exploring approaches fits P15 best.
units.anchor: Goblin.tools has a “Magic ToDo”, which can help you break down more complicated tasks
units.fit_note: Task planning rather than idea generation; also names a recommended tool.

units.why: Allows AI in 'the initial stages' of assignments but requires work to 'go beyond the Generative AI output'; brainstorming and outlining allowed (P15) with a keep-thinking condition.
units.anchor: you must ensure that your work goes beyond the Generative AI output.

units.why: Defines brainstorming as 'thinking with Generative AI, rather than having Generative AI think for you'; students stay primary thinker (P32).
units.anchor: brainstorming means thinking with Generative AI, rather than having Generative AI think for you.

units.why: Gives advice on writing better prompts with context and own ideas, matching P93.
units.anchor: you should provide more context in your prompt, share your interests, your ideas

units.why: The course will use AI research tools 'to find additional sources'; AI for literature search (P104).
units.anchor: We will explore ResearchRabbit, SemanticScholar, AI research assistants in e-books

units.why: Limits to 'free Generative AI tools' or university-provided ones 'to ensure everyone has access to the same resources'; equitable access, no paid tools (P51).
units.anchor: you may only use free Generative AI tools, or those that are provided to you

units.why: Students must 'share your prompts, screenshots of your chats' and reflect on use; logs and reflections submitted (P26).
units.anchor: share your prompts, screenshots of your chats with Generative AI tools

units.why: The instructor will hold 'ongoing discussions in class' about AI use, explaining and discussing rules (P66). Repeated in later examples; coded once here.
units.anchor: we will have ongoing discussions in class about effective use of Generative AI

units.why: Despite the planning allowance, 'you should not use AI to draft or revise your writing'; AI for prose is not allowed (P19), set separately from planning.
units.anchor: you should not use AI to draft or revise your writing.

units.why: AI is prohibited for 'in-class quizzes, midterms, or finals'; exam ban (P22). Recurs in later examples; coded once.
units.anchor: such as in-class quizzes, midterms, or finals, where Generative AI usage is prohibited.

units.why: Instructor commits to stating in the assignment when AI is prohibited; per-assignment communication (P09).
units.anchor: I will clearly state this on any relevant assignment.

units.why: AI use in prohibited assessments 'will be considered a violation of the academic integrity policy'; misconduct classification (P36).
units.anchor: will be considered a violation of the academic integrity policy.

units.why: Students are 'responsible for the accuracy of anything you submit' and 'must read the material you are citing'; ownership of submitted work (P29), verification also implied (P31).
units.anchor: you will be responsible for the accuracy of anything you submit

units.why: Fabricated data or research from AI 'may result in an academic integrity violation for falsifying information'; misconduct (P36); P74 would be a ban on fabrication but this is a consequence statement.

units.why: Instructor commits to 'clearly disclosing when I use it and why'; disclosure of instructor AI use (P47), with modeling (P112) secondary.
units.anchor: I will model appropriate Generative AI usage by clearly disclosing when I use it and

units.why: Lists instructor uses of AI such as restructuring lectures and finding articles; instructor AI use for teaching work (P59).

units.why: Instructor promises to 'never use Generative AI to grade your work'; humans assign grades (P46); the communication clause is part of the same commitment.
units.anchor: I will never use Generative AI to grade your work or to communicate with you.
units.fit_note: Also bars AI in instructor communication with students.

units.why: AI is useful 'as long as you also develop and apply the skills' to 'assess and revise' output; verify and evaluate output (P31).

units.why: Allows AI for revising a second draft only after writing the first draft yourself; a do-it-first sequencing rule (P90).

notes: Coded two included university-layer CFE documents. Samples in the policy-examples document repeat some sentences across examples (class discussion, exam prohibition, consequences wording); these are coded once. KB 3406 student guidelines were inaccessible per collect notes.
